conclusions: Jinja gains its missing BaseLoader.load group by admitting the original raw-rank16 full window; it is an allocation gain, not new retrieval or repaired clipping.

Mutation.execute is present at raw rank11, in the portfolio, canonical selected pool and actual returned backfill pool. It never enters proposed eligible or delivered results. A raw-rank45 MutationObserver.reset admission consumes a surviving slot, then unchanged backfill re-adds the evicted QueryClient row and fills the eight-row cap before reaching Mutation.execute. No character/token clipping caused the two lost groups.

The reset comment contains the rare query term another (df1), and its identifier contributes current. Its second-aspect lexical support exceeds the actual reference even while required Mutation.execute behavior disappears. A lexical aspect floor is not a behavior-preservation guarantee.

The missing Mutation.execute reference row is outside the frozen protected ID/definition/window subset. Actual protected rows remain covered, so both source and lexical guards truthfully accept. The Jinja gain also replaces two unprotected actual coverage rows: observed all-source preservation is6/8 for Jinja and7/8 for the loss case, both with8 delivered rows.

The optimistic-result query gains one exact group through a rank16 first createResult window, but fetchState and the later createResult evidence remain undelivered; it is not an additional completed behavior.

All detailed delivered rows retain original literal source/hash/provenance and original raw or owner-inherited scalars. The failure is relevance/composition, not fabricated source, score drift or runtime corruption.
next_design_implication: Study allocation together with the actual coverage backfill contributions and lexical false-positive mechanisms under the same context cap. The protected subset and per-aspect maxima do not certify arbitrary baseline behavior.
